Enhancing Explainability in Credit Scoring with Interpretable Machine Learning DENIS BURAKOV In this paper, we show, using a synthetic dataset created by blending real-world credit risk data, that when responsibly designed and properly constrained, Machine Learning (ML) models used for credit scoring – under certain conditions – outperform their linear alternatives both in terms of discriminatory power and calibration accuracy while remaining highly interpretable. The design of ML models discussed in this paper may provide a compelling case for conservative lenders to begin transitioning toward more advanced algorithms without having to compromise on the balance between explainability and accuracy. 1 INTRODUCTION Credit scoring is a regulated, high-risk application of machine learning used primarily in Financial Services. Credit scoring became one of the most successful predictive modeling use-cases and revolutionized consumer lending helping banks to immediately become more profitable [3]. Areas of application of scoring models include loan application and behavioral scoring, risk segmentation, and pricing among other internal uses. Notwithstanding economic gains, credit scoring models are replete with model risk. An incorrect use of a credit scoring model (e.g., caused by poor model design or low quality and non-representative data) can harm customers at scale and expose a lender to legal risks. As a result, comprehensive regulatory frameworks have been established to safeguard consumers from the failure of automated decision-making. In banking, the golden standard of a standardized credit risk assessment is the logistic regression model, often advanced via a supervised binning technique called Weight-of-Evidence (WOE). A "gold standard" scorecard produced via this modeling technique is an additive model with a small number of main effects (deviations from this may result in less interpretable models). Therefore, such models may struggle to capture all the complex interactions within the data, which results in costly manual feature engineering to improve model performance. In other domains, researchers frequently emphasize the superior performance of tree-based models, particularly gradient boosted trees, over linear [4] and deep learning models on tabular data [13]. Despite the impressive success in other domains, the adoption of tree-based models for risk management purposes lags behind their scope of application in other fields due to reasons of data quality, explainability, and IT-infrastructure [21]. The key reason behind this gap, primarily for credit risk management [21] and in the Financial services in general [11], is a prevailing sentiment among regulators and model risk managers that Boosting / Random Forest models are intrinsically opaque or "black-box" thus rendering them unsuitable for high-stakes decision-making like lending. This concern has led to various efforts to enhance the interpretability of "black-box" models using tools like SHAP1 or surrogate modeling. In response, some ML practitioners have expressed concerns about the overall use of “black-box” ML for high-risk applications, as advocated by C. Rudin [22]. In this paper, building on prior studies [9], [8], [15], we show that tree-based credit scoring models can offer interpretability without compromising performance, challenging prevailing industry opinions. Utilizing a common scorecard methodology for explaining models to frontline staff, auditors, and regulators, we assess two tree-based model variants: Constrained2 XGBoost and an extension of XGBoost with random forests as base learners. Our goal is to illustrate that well-configured and effectively communicated tree-based ensemble models are suitable for credit scoring and can exhibit similar characteristics to linear scoring models. The methodology of credit risk modeling presented in this paper aims to shift the perception of tree-based ensemble models from being considered unsuitable to becoming an industry standard for assessing consumer credit risk. 2 DATASET ENGINEERING In this paper, a synthetic credit risk portfolio is engineered by combining data from three primary sources: dataset_A: FICO Explainable ML Challenge3. • Origin: FICO Explainable ML Challenge. • Loan purpose: Line-of-credit loans. • Target Variable: 90 days past due (DPD) over 24 months. dataset_B: Lending Club4. • Source: Lending Club. • Loan purpose: Line-of-credit and installment loans. • Target Variable: 90 days past due (DPD) over 24 months. dataset_C: Give Me Some Credit5. • Source: Kaggle. • Loan purpose: Line-of-credit and installment loans. • Target Variable: 90 days past due (DPD) over 24 months. The first dataset describes the application scoring process (applying for a home credit line), the other two describe behavioral scoring (customers who were approved to use a lending product) and include line-of-credit and installment product types. Combined together, they form a synthetic end-to-end credit scoring dataset incorporating application and behavioral stages of the loan lifecycle. In addition, a similar operationalization of the target variable in the three datasets allows to model the horizon of into-default event consistently. Risk drivers include balances and credit line utilization, credit bureau scores, socio-demographic information from the application form as well as some other indicators related to a product mix of a customer. A full list of selected risk drivers is available in Table 4, including monotonic constraints (business logic) and inclusion of specific features into the blended dataset. We use 10% default rate to reduce the effect of class imbalance on predictive accuracy following recent research in this area [7]. An experimental dataset generation process consists of two major steps: random sampling of defaulted labels from the three datasets and stacking them together with randomly sampled features across horizontal axis as shown in Figure 1. This approach can be extended to generate datasets with other target variables relevant for credit risk modeling (e.g., loss given default, credit loss) using stratification based on a binary target variable. Combining the defaulted and non-defaulted datasets together allows us to create a synthetic scoring dataset with a 10% default rate to be used in the modeling process. 3 MODELS 3.1 Baseline: WOE Logistic Regression The golden standard of a standardized risk assessment is a Weight-of-Evidence Logistic Regression (WOE LR) model. This model design has been in use for several decades and continues to be among the most interpretable and reliable methods in credit risk modeling. The outputs of WOE LR can be easily converted into a scorecard format helping to facilitate explainability of such models to end users. Supervised binning is the key component of a WOE LR model. During this process, a model developer transforms the raw values of candidate features into several bins, according to some business logic or splitting techniques (e.g., decision

4 Denis Burakov trees). The main idea of supervised binning is to find optimal cut-off points to define bins that ensure a balance between being "wide enough" and "narrow enough" by having distinctly different risk characteristics with minimum information loss [16]. Feature transformation consists in mapping its raw values to a bin’s corresponding Weight-of-Evidence (WOE) score. For each feature, WOE score for bin 𝑏𝑖 is calculated as follows: 𝑊𝑂𝐸𝑏𝑖 = log (%good𝑏𝑖 %bad𝑏𝑖 ) (1) In Equation 1, the numerator corresponds to the share (%) of good (non-defaulted) records in a bucket 𝑏𝑖 out of the total number of good (non-defaulted) records, and the denominator corresponds to the share (%) of bad (defaulted) observations in a bucket 𝑏𝑖 out of the total number of bad (defaulted) observations in the sample. The Weight-of-Evidence (WOE) score can take on any value. Positive WOE scores indicate that a particular bin has a lower default rate compared to the sample average default rate and has a higher default rate if WOE scores are negative. In machine learning terminology, a vector of WOE scores as an encoded feature can be thought of as a "weak learner", akin to a univariate decision tree [9]. After supervised binning is performed and features are transformed into WOE scores, a logistic regression model is estimated. The objective function of the model is to minimize the logistic cost function, or log loss (Equation 2),using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). The output of the logit function (Equation 3) is subsequently transformed into probabilities using a sigmoid (Equation 4) function. Log Loss = − 1 𝑁 𝑁∑︁ 𝑖=1 [𝑦𝑖 log(𝑝𝑖 ) + (1 − 𝑦𝑖 ) log(1 − 𝑝𝑖 )] (2) Log Loss (Equation 2) measures the accuracy of a credit scoring model by comparing its predicted probabilities to the actual outcomes. 𝑁 represents the total number of data points, 𝑖 is an index representing each data point, 𝑦𝑖 is the actual binary outcome (0 or 1) for the 𝑖-th data point, and 𝑝𝑖 is the predicted probability that the 𝑖-th data point belongs to the positive class (class 1). The Log Loss penalizes the model when it predicts the wrong class with a high probability. We estimate a WOE LR using OptBinning7 package that uses a specific set of constraints to be optimized during the supervised binning procedure. These constraints might range from requiring a minimum number of records per bin to monotonicity constraints. This variant of the binning process is known as the optimal binning process [19]. The optimal binning is generally solved by iteratively merging an initial granular discretization until imposed constraints are satisfied. Default parameters were used in the binning procedure starting with the maximum number of bins after pre- binning (max_n_prebins) being 20 and the fraction of minimum number of records for each prebin (min_prebin_size) being 5%. Additionally, expert-based monotonicity constraints were incorporated into the binning process via the binning_fit_params parameter. 3.2 Model 1: Constrained XGBoost XGBoost is an advanced Gradient Tree Boosting-based software that can efficiently handle large-scale ML tasks which has become the de facto method-of-the-first-choice for a majority of data science problems (Wang et al. 2020). XGBoost is made up of several decision trees, each of which is a weak learner, and Boosting technology promotes it to a strong learner [25]. In the context of binary classification, unless specified differently, XGBoost uses log loss (Equation 2) as an objective function. Binary classification trees are constructed sequentially, forming an ensemble of weak learner trees with the objective to minimize loss. Each successive tree in the ensemble aims to correct errors made by the previous trees by y working on the first (gradients) and second order (hessians) gradient statistics of the previous tree’s predictions. Each individual tree in the binary classification case produces log-odds scores (margins) for each tree’s leaf nodes, which are subsequently added together to produce the final prediction (Equation 5). A sigmoid transformation (Equation 4) is used to convert the resulting sum of margins into probabilities. An XGBoost tree ensemble model can be viewed as a function of the following form: 𝐺 (𝑃 (𝑌 = 1)) = 𝑀∑︁ 𝑗=1 𝐻 𝑗 (𝑥 𝑗 ) (5) Where 𝐻 𝑗 (𝑥 𝑗 ) represents an individual tree 𝑗 that is combined into the final prediction (𝐺 (𝑃 (𝑌 = 1))). XGBoost’s objective function optimized during training can be expressed using Equation 6 adapted from [6]: obj(𝑡) = 𝑀∑︁ 𝑗=1 ( 𝑦𝑖 , 𝑦 (𝑡−1) 𝑖 + 𝐻 𝑗 (𝑥 𝑗 ) ) + Ω(𝐻 𝑗 (𝑥 𝑗 )) (6) Where Ω is a regularization term to control for complexity of trees to avoid overfitting. The newer version of XGBoost, referred to as Constrained XGBoost, incorporates monotonic constraints [20], allowing users to enforce monotonic relationships between model inputs and predictions [15]. These constraints prevent splits on monotonic features that could violate the constraints, enabling the incorporation of causal knowledge (e.g., monotonic relationships) by domain experts into the modeled relationships (e.g., higher debt-to-income ratios indicating higher risk). 7OptBinning: The Python Optimal Binning library http://gnpalencia.org/optbinning/ http://gnpalencia.org/optbinning/

6 Denis Burakov Another customization option for XGBoost models involves using random forest base learners. These learners are particularly appealing for credit risk modeling as they enable the creation of multiple sub-models at each tree iteration in gradient boosting. Domain experts can assess various randomly constructed trees to derive new features based on variable interactions within trees or aggregate predictions from promising tree candidates into a new model. Random forests may be implemented in XGBoost as base learners by setting num_parallel_tree parameter equal to an integer greater than 1. The idea is that each boosting round will no longer consist of one tree, but a number of parallel trees, which in turn make up a forest [24]. It is important to note in this case that the number of trees being constructed is derived as num_parallel_tree × n_estimators. Therefore, with 50 iterations and 2 trees per iteration we will have built 100 trees. Table 1. We follow applied conventions of using two metrics to assess rank-ordering power and evaluate the accuracy of probabilistic predictions. Empirical results were obtained from calculating metrics on a holdout set (30%). 4.1 Discriminatory power Discriminatory power measures the rank-ordering ability of a model in order to quantify its ability at differentiating good and bad risk. In credit risk, the most commonly used metric for assessing discriminatory power is the Gini score sometimes also denoted in the risk literature as Accuracy Ratio [10], [23]. Gini = 𝑃 [𝑆𝐷 < 𝑆𝑁 ] − 𝑃 [𝑆𝐷 > 𝑆𝑁 ] (7) In Equation 7, the Gini score represents a probability that a randomly chosen example from a positive class (defaulted, 𝑆𝐷 ) is ranked higher than a randomly chosen example from the negative class (non-defaulted, 𝑆𝑁 ) by a scoring model. The closer the Gini score is to one the better. AUC score can be derived from the Gini score and vice versa as follows: AUC = (1 + Gini) / 2, Gini = 2 * AUC - 1. 4.2 Calibration accuracy A significant drawback of rank-ordering metrics like the Gini score is their inability to assess the actual accuracy of the probabilistic predictions. To address this concern, model calibration accuracy is assessed separately by categorizing predictions into bins (or risk grades) and applying various statistical tests. A common metric used in measuring the calibration of probabilistic predictions without assigning a subjective number of bins is the Brier score [5]. Brier score is a proper scoring rule that equates to Mean Squared Error (MSE) for binary classification. Brier score can be decomposed into calibration and refinement loss [18], [2], [12], [1] shown in Equations 9 and 10. Brier score = 1 𝑛 𝑛∑︁ 𝑗=1 (𝑦 𝑗 − 𝑝 𝑗 )2 (8)

8 Denis Burakov Calibration loss = 1 𝑛 𝑛∑︁ 𝑘=1 ∑︁ 𝑗=𝑛𝑖 (𝑟𝑖 − 𝑝𝑖 )2 (9) Refinement loss = 1 𝑛 𝑛∑︁ 𝑘=1 ∑︁ 𝑗=𝑛𝑖 𝑟𝑖 (1 − 𝑟𝑖 ) (10) The Brier score in Equation 8 measures the mean squared error between actual outcomes (𝑦 𝑗 ) and predicted probabilities (𝑝 𝑗 ) for each data point. 𝑟𝑖 in Equations 9 and 10 corresponds to average event (default) rate while 𝑝𝑖 corresponds to average predicted probability (of default) for each unique ROC segment. The partitioning of the Brier score allows us to establish a calibration loss metric, which calculates the mean squared deviation from empirical probabilities based on ROC segments (L1 norm). Alternatively, we can adjust the formula in Equation 9 to derive the mean absolute error, L2 norm. This metric definition is conceptually related to Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as in [14], but in this paper it is measured at the ROC segment level without discretizing predictions into bins. We then derive the calibration score as 1 – ECE, offering a way to evaluate predictive performance similar to the Gini score’s role in conveying model performance to business stakeholders. Visual representation still employs equally distributed bins in a calibration curve diagram. 4.3 Experimental results The Cumulative Accuracy Profile (CAP) curve in the left hand-side plot of Figure 2 shows discriminatory power for the three scoring models. This feature describes a number of credit cards a customer has and has an increasing risk trend with regards to default risk. Feature account_never_delinq_percent was not included in the WOE LR model’s short-list due to a zero coefficient. Additionally, it can be seen from the scorecard plots in Figure 5 that there are two distributions of good risk in the Constrained RF XGBoost scorecard (more pronounced than in the Constrained XGBoost score distribution). The distributions shown in Figure 5 indicate possible alternative score cut-offs that a lender can employ to perform underwriting policy testing. 6 CONCLUSION Drawing upon previous studies [9], [8], [15], this study demonstrates using a synthetic dataset created by blending real-world credit risk data that when responsibly designed and properly constrained, tree-based ML models for credit scoring – under certain assumptions – outperform their linear alternatives both in terms of discriminatory power and calibration accuracy while remaining highly interpretable. A method of transforming tree-based models into scorecards discussed in this paper may promote acceptance of such models in decision-making and make a compelling case for cautious lenders to begin using more advanced algorithms without having to compromise on the balance between explainability and accuracy. This research underscores the potential of ML to further revolutionize consumer lending, offering a bridge between traditional risk assessment methods and cutting-edge predictive models. By drawing from the principles of responsible design and explainability, lenders can harness the full potential of ML models in credit risk management, contributing to more robust, efficient, and profitable lending practices. 7 ACKNOWLEDGMENTS The author would like to thank Paul Edwards for providing helpful critique on the draft and sharing the approach, Alexey Calabourdin (a.calabourdin@gmail.com) for helpful tips on calibration and sharing the Brier score decomposition code, Fabiana Clemente and and Guillermo Navas-Palencia for providing inputs on the draft.
